hints: Focus on the job of NaOH here, it can act as a nucleophile for substitution or as a base for elimination depending on the solvent.
Remember that aqueous NaOH favours substitution to an alcohol, while ethanolic NaOH favours elimination to an alkene.
Check if bromoethane with only one Br atom could ever give a molecule with two OH groups in one step.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two competing reactions**

Haloalkanes like bromoethane can do substitution or elimination with NaOH. Aqueous conditions favour substitution, ethanolic conditions favour elimination.

Substitution: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$

Elimination: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Br}^-$

**Check row 1: water to ethan-1,2-diol**

Ethan-1,2-diol is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, it has two OH groups. Bromoethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, has only one Br to replace, so one step can only introduce one OH. Row 1 is incorrect.

**Check row 2: ethanol to ethene**

NaOH in ethanol acts as a base and removes HBr from bromoethane. This is dehydrohalogenation (elimination) to form the alkene ethene. Row 2 is correct.

**Check row 3: water to ethanol**

NaOH in water (aqueous) acts as a nucleophile. $\text{OH}^-$ replaces $\text{Br}$ by nucleophilic substitution to form ethanol. Row 3 is correct.

So only rows 2 and 3 are correct.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes row 1. Ethan-1,2-diol needs two functional groups, but bromoethane has only one C-Br bond, so aqueous NaOH can only give the mono-alcohol ethanol, not a diol.
options.B: Incorrect because it includes row 1 and misses row 3. Row 1 is impossible (no source of a second OH group), while row 3 is the classic aqueous substitution to ethanol and should be included.
options.C: Correct because rows 2 and 3 are both right. Row 2 is elimination with ethanolic NaOH to ethene, and row 3 is nucleophilic substitution with aqueous NaOH to ethanol. Row 1 is wrong.
options.D: Incorrect because it misses row 2. Aqueous NaOH does give ethanol (row 3 is right), but ethanolic NaOH definitely gives ethene by elimination (row 2 is also right), so both 2 and 3 are needed.
